cases.abstract: Low-rank adaptation saves parameters, yet the same factors must adjust both the lengths and directions of pretrained weight columns. A VL-BART checkpoint analysis finds these changes positively correlated under LoRA but negatively correlated under full fine-tuning, motivating Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA). DoRA learns a separate column magnitude vector and applies low-rank updates to normalized directions, making column length adjustable without a dense trainable matrix. The adapted weights can be merged before inference. Across eight commonsense benchmarks with pooled training data, LLaMA-7B achieves 78.4% mean accuracy versus 74.7% for a LoRA baseline reported in prior work, using trainable parameter fractions of 0.84% and 0.83%, respectively. DoRA follows the baseline configuration but adjusts the learning rate; halving its rank yields 77.5% accuracy with 0.43% trainable parameters. Image- and video-text scores also improve over reported LoRA baselines, although the video aggregate remains below full fine-tuning. Detaching the normalization denominator lowers training memory relative to unmodified DoRA with small score changes. These comparisons support separating magnitude learning from low-rank directional adaptation to improve the tested accuracy-parameter tradeoff.
cases.methods: DoRA separates two jobs that an ordinary low-rank update performs together: changing a weight column's length and changing its direction. It constructs each adapted column from the corresponding column of W0 + BA, divides by that column's norm, and multiplies by a learned scalar. The pretrained matrix W0 stays frozen; the magnitude scalars start at its column norms, and zero initialization of B preserves the original weights before training. Normalization therefore lets the small magnitude vector control column lengths while the trainable low-rank factors alter directions. In the exact derivative, the gradient with respect to the unnormalized direction is scaled and projected perpendicular to the current direction. The experiments detach the denominator to reduce backpropagation memory: its value tracks the updated factors, but its derivative is omitted. This keeps the forward separation of magnitude and direction while replacing the projected directional gradient with a scaled gradient.
cases.results: DoRA's advantage in the LLaMA-7B rank sweep is not simply a consequence of training more parameters. Across eight commonsense tests, rank-8 DoRA averages 77.9% accuracy against LoRA's 40.7%, with trainable fractions of 0.22% and 0.21%. It also exceeds rank-32 LoRA's 74.7%, supporting a better accuracy-parameter tradeoff under the reported recipes, although learning rates can differ. More rank does not ensure more accuracy: DoRA scores 61.9% at rank 4 and 72.1% at rank 64, versus 78.4% at rank 32. Multimodal results further distinguish improvement over LoRA from recovery of full fine-tuning performance. On VL-BART video tasks, DoRA raises the aggregate from the reported LoRA baseline's 83.5 to 85.4, but full fine-tuning remains higher at 87.5. Because this aggregate mixes question-answering and captioning metrics, the comparison supports better benchmark scores rather than a uniform accuracy increase. Thus parameter efficiency improves in these comparisons without eliminating either rank sensitivity or the remaining video-task gap.
cases.notes: Retained the initial evidence choices. Table 1 supports near-equal-parameter and halved-rank comparisons; Table 15 supports rank sensitivity; Table 3 qualifies recovery of full fine-tuning. Commonsense and VL-BART baselines come from prior work, and DoRA learning rates may differ. Checkpoint correlations motivate the design but do not isolate the source of accuracy gains. Equations 6 and 11 distinguish exact and detached-denominator gradients. Use table entries where narrative summaries disagree: halved-rank LLaMA-13B scores 80.8 versus LoRA's 80.5, and Table 7 reports VL-BART 77.3 without detachment versus 77.4 with it. Keep the overhead ablation separate from Table 1; infer no statistical significance.

cases.abstract: Optimizer-state compression need not require a low-rank parameterization of the weights. GaLore projects gradients into a compact subspace, maintains optimizer statistics there, and expands each update onto dense weights. Periodically refreshing the projection lets accumulated updates move beyond one fixed subspace. The analysis bounds gradient stable rank under specified forms and conditions and establishes conditional contraction of the projected gradient with fixed projections and an identity regularizer; these guarantees do not cover the refreshed Adam implementation. In C4 pretraining, a 1B model reaches validation perplexity 15.64, versus 15.56 for full-rank Adam and 19.21 for rank-matched LoRA with frozen initial weights, with equal learning-rate search budgets. A separate single-trial 7B run reaches 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam after 19.7 billion tokens on 64 A100 GPUs. Single-device profiling combines projection, 8-bit optimization, and per-layer updates to fit 7B training within 22.0 GB at small token batches, without offloading or checkpointing. The results support gradient compression for memory-constrained dense-weight training with close observed perplexity, while exposing a throughput cost relative to 8-bit Adam.
cases.methods: GaLore reduces Adam's storage by compressing gradient statistics while keeping the weights dense. For a gradient G of an m-by-n matrix with m <= n, it uses the leading r left singular vectors as a projection P and forms R = P^T G. Adam stores its two moment arrays in this r-by-n space; the resulting update is scaled and multiplied by P before modifying the weights. Recomputing P periodically lets successive updates occupy different subspaces, so their sum is not restricted to one rank-r factorization. The theorem for fixed projections and an identity regularizer establishes conditional contraction only of the projected gradient, not convergence of this refreshed Adam procedure. The refresh therefore serves an operational purpose that the theorem cannot ensure: following useful directions as the gradient subspace changes. Rare refreshes can retain an unhelpful subspace; frequent ones add decomposition cost and may disrupt accumulated optimizer statistics.
cases.results: The measured 22.0 GB footprint of 8-bit GaLore for 7B training makes small token batches feasible within a 24 GB memory budget, but it reflects more than gradient projection. Relative to BF16 Adam and 8-bit Adam, the reductions are 63.3% and 52.3%, respectively, in single-device profiling without checkpointing or offloading. Projection reduces optimizer-state storage, and per-layer updates avoid retaining all gradients. The close perplexity result comes from a separate experiment: a single trial on 64 A100 GPUs reaches 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam after 19.7 billion tokens. It supports close observed performance, not statistical equivalence or demonstrated complete pretraining on a consumer GPU. Throughput also constrains the memory benefit. At a 256-token batch for a 1B model, with both methods using per-layer updates, 8-bit GaLore processes 1019.63 tokens per second versus 1205.31 for 8-bit Adam. The benefit is therefore access to a lower-memory training regime, with a throughput penalty in the measured implementation.
cases.notes: Retained the initial separation between optimizer compression, fixed-projection theory, and system profiling. Theorem 3.8 requires the stated gradient form, Lipschitz continuity, bounded weights, fixed projections, an identity regularizer, and a positive contraction margin; it does not prove global loss convergence for Adam with refreshed bases. Table 2 provides C4 perplexities and parameter-plus-optimizer memory estimates, not total device usage. Section 5.3/Table 3 supply the separate single-trial 64-A100 result. Figure 4/Section 5.5 support the combined 22.0 GB footprint; Table 11 supplies throughput with per-layer mode matched. Do not merge smaller-model token counts that disagree between Tables 2 and 5 or infer statistical equivalence.
